newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Independent ECB essential for EMU-Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Independent ECB essential for EMU-Tietmeyer.

text.p: German Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Wednesday lashed out at attempts to undermine the independence of Europe's future central bank, saying it was an absolute prerequisite for a stable single European currency.

In a speech at a ceremony in Bonn for the 100th anniversary of the birth of former economics minister Ludwig Erhard, Tietmeyer said there should be no doubt that the central bank had to be independent of all political forces.
"No one should doubt this, whatever his arguments or additional ideas," he said, according to an advance text.

Tietmeyer's forceful comments come as Germany's closest European ally, France, was leading a drive to create a political counterpart to the European Central Bank, which will handle monetary policy once the new euro has been created in 1999.
The fiercely-independent Bundesbank is wary of such plans, feeling such a group could put political pressure on the new central bank and hinder its anti-inflationary policies.
Tietmeyer recalled Bonn had planned such a group for the Bundesbank but Erhard, the father of the deutschemark in 1948 and the 1950s "economic miracle," opposed it and won the day.

French assurances that the proposed economic council would only be an informal body have done little to assuage German worries that Paris really sees the council as a way to control the exchange rate -- and the ECB -- through the back door.

Without refering specifically to the French proposal, Tietmeyer issued a clear warning that ideas of this type could damage the credibility of the ECB's policies by suggesting that governments only tolerated its independence under suffrance.
"The dangers of the proposed European System of Central Banks having an independence which is accepted only formally and reluctantly should also not be underestimated," he said.
"A hidden dissent could place a considerable burden on the necessary credibility of the European Central Bank, not to speak of the monetary union's later susceptibility to conflict," he added.

Tietmeyer noted that the blueprint laid down for the ECB in the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union made absolutely clear that price stability had to be the European bank's number one priority.
"Germany's experience was evidently the force behind the formulation of the Maastricht Treaty," he added.

Attacking suggestions that the euro area must have some form of exchange rate targeting policy, Tietmeyer said that the ECB, like the Bundesbank, must have internal and not external stability as its priority.
Stressing the need for the European central bank to have a credible monetary policy, he said that the euro could otherwise fail to establish itself as stable currency.

"And the hope, which I also cherish, that the euro will fluctuate less against the dollar and yen than the mark -- this hope could easily turn into the opposite," he said, according to a text of his speech.

"If the European Central Bank should be hindered in gaining the necessary credibility in markets, then the euro could easily waft to and fro on the currency markets, like reeds in the wind," he added.
Germany and France are each seen as essential founder members of the single currency block, although both have their work cut out to meet the economic targets for entry this year.
Both Tietmeyer and a second Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said they nonetheless expected Germany to make the grade. "The chances are good," Tietmeyer said.
